newsitem.title: UK: UK brewers disappointed by tax freeze on beer.
newsitem.headline: UK brewers disappointed by tax freeze on beer.

text.p: Britain's beer industry said on Tuesday it was disappointed by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's budget statement, which froze tax duty paid on beer and wine for the second year running.

"We are disappointed with this budget. We think that freezing the duty will not solve the problem of smuggling and cross-border shopping," said Brian Finnerty, a spokesman for the Brewers and Licensed Retailers Association.
British drinkers pay about seven times more tax on a pint of beer than their French counterparts. British duty on a pint of five percent alcohol by volume is 30 pence.

In France it is just four pence, encouraging people to buy their beer in mainland Europe. The BLRA estimate the total volume of duty paid beer flooding into the country is about 4-1/2 percent of the total beer market. Over half of this is for illegal resale.
A spokeswoman for Scottish & Newcastle said the company was "very disappointed" that Clarke had failed to move towards bringing UK duty rate in line with the rest of Europe.

"Commendably the Chancellor acknowledges that other governments discriminate against our whisky exports -- how surprising then that our own government is so willing to discriminate against the UK beer industry," said S&N chief executive Brian Stewart.
The BLRA warned that the freeze will force more to close with the loss of more jobs in the industry while crime and fraud will grow. Clarke raised the duty on beer by 2p a pint in 1994.
"The proportion of tax on the price of a pint in the pub is now at its lowest level for thirty years," said the Chancellor in his budget statement.
S&N shares rose 5-1/2p to 652p, Whitbread was up 4p at 755p.

Bass shares were off 11p at 816-1/2 at the close on Tuesday after Clarke announced an increase of over 40 percent on tax on alcoholic soft drinks, known as "alcopops", from January 1. The increase is expected to hit sales of Bass's Hoopers Hooch brand.

A spokesman for Bass said, "We are intensely disappointed that he has reduced tax on one drink and in the same breath not lowered tax on beer by the same amount and actually increased it on flavoured alcoholic beverages."
He added, "The rationale for taxing flavoured alcoholic beverages seems somewhat suspect, it does not seem to have an economic or social basis. It's a big revenue opportunity so he's taxed it."
A spokesman for the Wine and Spirits Association said the freeze in duty on wine for the second year runnning will hit the small wine trader especially hard.

"We were pretty devastated because there were a lot of signs he (Clarke) understood the issue of cross-border shopping but there has been no move towards practical help for the trade," said Barry Sutton, deputy chairman of the Association.
